title: Vyasa sends Arjuna to the gods
hookLine: Vyasa walks into the stuck camp with a plan, not a miracle: Arjuna must climb to the gods for their weapons
carry: grace meets effort: pray, then climb
tomorrow: what does a holy man ask Arjuna to throw away?

cards: An old sage walks into a stuck camp. Bhima wants them stronger, and soon. Yudhishthira won't break his word, and he knows how formidable the warriors on the other side are.
The brothers are caught between impatience and patience. The visitor is Vyasa, grandfather of both the Pandavas and the Kauravas, and he has come with a way out.

teach.b: Vyasa takes Yudhishthira aside. I know what's in your heart, he says: the fear of Bhishma and Drona and Karna. So here's what to do.
He gives Yudhishthira a sacred knowledge to teach to Arjuna, an inner discipline that will let him reach the gods.

teach.h: SEEK THE WEAPONS OF THE GODS.
teach.b: Arjuna must go, he says, and seek out the gods themselves, Indra and Rudra and the guardians of the world, and win their weapons through ascetic effort. That is how the Pandavas will be ready when the exile ends.
Look at what Vyasa doesn't do. He doesn't bring the gods to the forest or end the exile with a miracle. The weapons are the gods' gifts, real grace, but Arjuna has to climb to them.
Hindu teachers have long held two things together: daiva, what the gods and fate give, and purushakara, human effort. The epic weighs them more than once, and many teachers read its answer as both.

It's why a Hindu student lights a lamp to Sarasvati, goddess of learning, before an exam, and still studies all week; why a family breaks a coconut before Ganesha to open a new shop, and then opens it at dawn.
Prayer isn't a shortcut, and effort isn't the whole story.
And notice the cost. Arjuna has to go alone. Yudhishthira teaches him what Vyasa taught, and Arjuna sets out, armed, toward the mountains of the north, with Draupadi's blessing on the road.

how: Retellings of the Mahabharata mark Vyasa's visit as the turn in the forest years, when Arjuna leaves to seek divine weapons; Hindu teaching often pairs daiva, what the gods give, with human effort, and many Hindus pray before a task and then work at it.

o: the sacred knowledge Vyasa gives the eldest
the northern mountains where gods give weapons
the forest of exile that turns into a base camp

games.q: the visit of Vyasa — tap the pairs.
p: must climb alone to seek the gods
grace meets the one who climbs

s: Vyasa ended the exile with a miracle
he kept the terms; the gods' weapons had to be won by Arjuna's own climb.
in Hindu teaching, prayer and effort work together
daiva, what the gods give, and purushakara, human effort: the epic's usual answer is both.
all five brothers went to seek the gods' weapons

games.q: a friend says if you pray before an exam, studying just shows you don't trust God. by Vyasa's plan, what's closer to Hindu teaching?
o: pray and study: the gods' grace meets your effort.
pray only; effort shows a lack of faith.
games.why: Vyasa didn't end the exile by miracle. the gods' weapons were real grace, and Arjuna still had to climb to them.

practice: Bring to mind one task ahead of you, something you can't hurry. Many Hindus begin a task with a short prayer, to Ganesha who clears the way or to Sarasvati for learning, and then get to work.
Try that shape now: breathe in and offer the task; breathe out and name one step you'll take today. If you don't pray, set the intention instead, and then name the step.

wordCard.voice: Vana. The forest of exile, which becomes a base camp the day Vyasa sends Arjuna to climb to the gods.

orig.note: Sanskrit Vyāsa: the sage who visits the camp, named by tradition as the composer of the Mahabharata.

carryVoice: Your line: grace meets effort: pray, then climb. Vyasa didn't shorten the exile; he gave it a climb. Tomorrow: what does a holy man ask Arjuna to throw away? See you then.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), Vyasa's visit to the Pandavas (the knowledge given to Yudhishthira for Arjuna; Arjuna sent to obtain weapons from the gods; Arjuna's departure and Draupadi's blessing)
